statement: A ticket machine takes only 5-cent, 10-cent and 20-cent coins. In how many different ways can you put in exactly 50 cents, if only the number of each coin matters and not the order?

choices.misconception: I only counted the ways that use no 20-cent coin at all.
I listed the ways but missed the one that uses only 5-cent coins.
I counted the ways with no 20-cent coin and with one, but forgot the ways with two.
I thought every way had to use at least one coin of each kind.

hints: Sort the ways by how many 20-cent coins they use.
Systematic listing: fix the biggest coin first, then the next biggest, and let the 5-cent coins fill whatever is left. Each case becomes a short, complete list you can check.
With no 20s, use 0 to 5 tens. With one 20, 30 cents remain: 0 to 3 tens. With two 20s, 10 cents remain: 0 or 1 ten.

solutions.reliable: Fix the number of 20-cent coins. None: the 10-cent coins can number 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, with 5-cent coins making up the rest, so 6 ways. One: 30 cents remain, and 0 to 3 tens gives 4 ways. Two: 10 cents remain, and 0 or 1 ten gives 2 ways. Total 6 + 4 + 2 = 12. The transferable idea: list by the largest item first, so each case is short and nothing is missed or repeated.
solutions.elegant: Once the 20s and 10s are chosen, the 5-cent coins are forced, so you are really counting how many tens fit in 50, 30 and 10 cents: 6 + 4 + 2.

whyOnTest: Listing a small set of combinations without gaps or repeats is the core skill, and the trap is a missing case at one end of a list.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
